nameStory: The Chrome-footed Bolete gets its striking name from its stem, which gleams with bright yellow coloration that resembles polished chrome. When you spot one in the forest, that brilliant yellow 'foot' catches your eye like a shiny piece of metal among the fallen leaves.
description: The Chrome-footed Bolete is a medium-sized mushroom with a reddish-brown cap and the signature bright yellow stem that gives it its name. Like all boletes, it has tiny pores under the cap instead of gills, creating a sponge-like surface. These mushrooms typically grow 3-6 inches tall with caps reaching 2-5 inches across, making them a noticeable find on the forest floor.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Bright chrome-yellow coloration, especially vibrant when fresh and young. The stem feels firm and solid, often with a slightly sticky or tacky texture when moist.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Reddish-brown to chocolate brown, feeling velvety or suede-like when dry. The surface may crack slightly in dry weather, revealing yellowish flesh underneath.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Yellow pore surface that may bruise blue-green when pressed or damaged. The pores are tiny and round, giving the underside a fine, spongy appearance.

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Cut flesh turns blue when exposed to air, then fades to yellow-brown. This color change happens within minutes of cutting or bruising.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Mild, pleasant mushroomy odor with no unpleasant or chemical notes. Some describe a slightly fruity or nutty scent when fresh.

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Olive-brown to dark brown spore print. Always obtain a spore print for positive identification, and never eat any wild mushroom without expert confirmation.

habitat: Found in mixed hardwood-conifer forests throughout New England, particularly associated with oak, beech, and pine trees. These boletes form partnerships with tree roots (mycorrhizal relationship) and prefer well-drained, acidic soils. Look for them in mature forests with rich leaf litter, often on slopes or near the base of large trees.

seasonality.spring: Not typically fruiting yet, though mycelial networks are active underground preparing for summer growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season from July through August, especially after warm summer rains. Fresh specimens show the brightest yellow stem coloration.
seasonality.fall: Continued fruiting into early fall, though specimens may be past their prime. Colors may be duller and stems less vibrant yellow.
seasonality.winter: No active fruiting, with only dried remnants occasionally visible on the forest floor.

funFact: The Chrome-footed Bolete's brilliant yellow stem contains compounds that were once investigated for natural dye production, capable of creating vibrant yellow and orange colors in wool and fabric.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other yellow-stemmed boletes, but the Chrome-footed's exceptionally bright, chrome-like yellow stem is more vivid than similar species. Remember: 'Chrome shines brightest' - if the yellow isn't eye-catchingly brilliant, it's probably a different bolete.
contextualKnowledge: This species was formerly classified in different genera before genetic studies placed it in the genus Harrya. Some older field guides may list it under previous scientific names, so don't be surprised if you see different classifications in various resources.
compareHints: Since it's the only Harrya species commonly found in New England, compare it with other yellow-stemmed boletes in the Boletaceae family. Chrome-footed Bolete's stem yellow is more intensely bright than the Butter Bolete's pale yellow or the Two-colored Bolete's more orange-yellow tones. The combination of reddish-brown cap and truly chrome-bright stem is distinctive among regional boletes.
